title: Victory as a funeral
hookLine: weapons are tools of ill omen; mark even victory with mourning (Tao Te Ching 31)

lines: WHO MOURNS AT A VICTORY PARADE?
A SIDE FOR FEASTS, A SIDE FOR FUNERALS.
THE WINNER STANDS WITH THE MOURNERS.
cards: Who mourns at a victory parade? Chapter thirty-one of the Tao Te Ching has an answer, and it's the general. Its instruction is about where people stand.

At a ceremony, there's a side for celebrations and a side for funerals. And the chapter puts the winning commander on the funeral side, as if the victory itself were a burial. Strange advice for a winner.

teach.h: ARMS, HOWEVER BEAUTIFUL, ARE ILL OMEN.
teach.b: First, the weapons. In James Legge's translation the chapter opens: "Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen." However beautiful.
A sword can be a lovely object, polished and balanced. The chapter doesn't deny it. It just won't let the beauty hide what the thing is for.

teach.h: ONLY WHEN THERE'S NO OTHER CHOICE.
teach.b: The wise person reaches for weapons only when there's no other choice, and even then puts calm and restraint first. The chapter doesn't pretend force is never needed.
It treats force as a last resort, picked up with reluctance.

Third, no joy in winning. Whoever delights in killing people, the chapter says, won't get what they want in the world. Victory isn't to be called beautiful, because calling it beautiful means taking pleasure in the dead.
Fourth, the funeral. The chapter says the left is the place of honor on festive occasions, and the right on occasions of mourning.

teach.h: THE GENERAL STANDS WITH THE MOURNERS.
teach.b: Then it places the commanding general on the right. Those who have killed many, it says, should weep for them, and the victor takes his place as if at the rites of mourning.
That's the title: victory as a funeral. Away from any battlefield, people still win things: an argument at dinner, a promotion someone else wanted, a point scored in front of a room.
The chapter doesn't say lose on purpose. It says notice who's on the other side of your win, and don't dance on the field.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-one as a call to use force only as a last resort and to grieve, not celebrate, what it costs, even in victory.

games.q: what does “victory as a funeral” mean?
o: a feast held to honor the soldiers who fell
the belief that every war ends in defeat
marking even a won battle with grief, not joy

p: the place of honor at festive occasions
the place of honor at mourning

s: chapter thirty-one says weapons must never be used
it says the wise reach for them only when there's no other choice, and put calm and restraint first.
the chapter tells the victor to celebrate
it says those who have killed many should weep, and the victor stands as if at the rites of mourning.
the chapter admits weapons can be beautiful
"arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen."

games.q: you've just won the battle, and the city wants a celebration in your honor. what does chapter thirty-one say to do?
o: stand where the mourners stand, and grieve the dead.
games.why: the chapter places the commanding general on the side of mourning and says the dead should be wept for. even a victory is a funeral.

practice: Bring to mind a disagreement you're likely to win; you have the facts. Now turn to the other person: what will they lose if you win loudly? Face, a little pride, the feeling of being heard.
Look for one way to make your point and leave them standing: a softer word, a question instead of a verdict.

wordCard.voice: Victory as a funeral. Chapter thirty-one's instruction that even a won battle be marked the way mourners mark a death, with the general standing on the side of grief. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: mourning rites, the way chapter thirty-one says even a victory should be kept.

carryVoice: Your line: win sadly. Someone is always on the other side of a win. Until tomorrow.
